Vertical integration is when one firm owns or merges with another firm at a DIFFERENT stage of the same supply chain (an upstream supplier or a downstream distributor/retailer), instead of merging with a direct competitor.

In the course materials: horizontal mergers are between direct competitors, while vertical mergers are between firms at different stages of production and distribution. Examples given include Comcast acquiring NBC content (content producer) and Netflix acquiring a movie studio.

One motivation is to coordinate pricing and decisions across stages (or capture production synergies), but it can raise regulatory scrutiny and add management complexity.

Coopetition means a relationship where firms BOTH cooperate and compete at the same time: they cooperate to CREATE value (grow the pie) and compete to CAPTURE value (divide the pie). In the course framing, every relationship has this duality, like customer-supplier pairs that collaborate on making the product but bargain hard on price.

A clean way to spot coopetition is to ask why cooperation helps: on the COST side, when $\text{Cost}(A\&B) < \text{Cost}(A) + \text{Cost}(B)$ (avoid duplication, gain speed, complementary assets); on the DEMAND side, when $\text{WTP}(A\&B) > \text{WTP}(A\mid \text{no }B) + \text{WTP}(B\mid \text{no }A)$ (their offerings raise each other’s value, like “common complements”).

The Phillips curve is the SHORT-RUN relationship between inflation $\\pi$ and unemployment $u$, drawn with $\\pi$ on the vertical axis and $u$ on the horizontal axis.

A compact way to write the idea is

$$
\\pi = f(u), \\quad f'(u) < 0 \\text{ (short run)}
$$

meaning higher inflation tends to be associated with lower unemployment in the short run (a downward-sloping curve in $\\pi$-$u$ space). The course materials also emphasize the “problem” policymakers made: treating that curve as fixed, even though expectations can adjust and shift the curve, with the economy tending back toward a “natural rate” of unemployment.

Cournot and Stackelberg are both quantity competition with identical products, but Cournot is simultaneous moves and Stackelberg is sequential moves (leader then follower).

Cournot setup (2 firms):
$$
\pi_i(q_i,q_j)=q_i P(q_i+q_j)-C_i(q_i)
$$
Best response comes from the FOC
$$
0=\frac{\partial \pi_i}{\partial q_i}=P(Q)+q_i P'(Q)-MC_i(q_i)
$$
where $Q=q_1+q_2$.

Stackelberg setup (firm 1 leads):
1. Follower (firm 2) chooses $q_2$ given $q_1$, so it uses the same FOC but treats $q_1$ as fixed and yields a best response function $q_2^*(q_1)$.
2. Leader anticipates that reaction and solves
$$
\max_{q_1}\; q_1 P(q_1+q_2^*(q_1)) - C_1(q_1).
$$

In the deck’s example, demand is $P(Q)=300-Q$ and $MC_1=MC_2=30$. First step: can you compute $P'(Q)$ for $P(Q)=300-Q$ and plug it into the follower’s FOC (leaving $q_1$ symbolic)?

Cournot and Bertrand differ in WHAT firms choose strategically.

1. Cournot: firms compete by choosing quantities $q_i$ (simultaneously or sequentially), typically with identical products. Given total quantity $Q=\sum_i q_i$, the market price is $p(Q)$, and each firm’s profit is

$$
\pi_i(q_i,q_{-i}) = \bigl(p(Q)-c\bigr)q_i.
$$

2. Bertrand: firms compete by choosing prices $p_i$ simultaneously, with identical products; the lowest price firm captures the market. In the basic Bertrand model (no capacity constraints), the Nash equilibrium drives prices to

$$
p=c,
$$

so profit is zero.

Big picture: Cournot “quantity competition” usually leaves $p>c$ and positive profit; Bertrand “price competition” creates a race-to-the-bottom to $p=c$ under the standard assumptions.

Logistic regression is a generalized linear model where you take a linear index and pass it through an S-shaped “link function” so the predicted values stay between 0 and 1 (unlike the linear probability model, which is just OLS on a binary $Y$ and can predict probabilities outside $[0,1]$).

The model is:

$$
p_i \equiv \Pr(Y_i=1\mid X_i)=F(X_i\beta)
$$

where the “index” is $X_i\beta$ and the logistic link is:

$$
F(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}
$$

Equivalently, it makes the log-odds linear in $X$:

$$
\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)=X_i\beta
$$

So a 1-unit increase in $X_k$ changes the log-odds by $\beta_k$, and changes the probability by a marginal effect that depends on where you are on the curve:

$$
\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial X_{ik}}=\beta_k\,p_i(1-p_i)
$$

In the course notes’ pictures, that’s why the “Logit” fit is curved and bounded in $[0,1]$, while the OLS prediction is a straight line that can go below 0 or above 1.

I can’t paste the course’s bootstrap section verbatim (copyright), but I can summarize what it covers and walk you through how to use it.

Bootstrap idea (what the section is teaching)
You approximate the sampling distribution of a statistic by re-sampling from your one observed dataset.

Nonparametric bootstrap procedure (as taught in the course materials)
1. Start with a dataset of $N$ observations.
2. Draw a “bootstrap sample” of size $N$ by sampling WITH replacement from the original data.
3. Recompute your statistic (mean, regression coefficient, etc.) on that bootstrap sample; call it $\hat\theta^{(b)}$.
4. Repeat for $b = 1,\dots,B$ (often a few thousand).
5. Use the variability of $\hat\theta^{(b)}$ across $b$ as the estimated uncertainty.

Bootstrap standard error (core formula)
Let $\hat\theta^{(1)},\dots,\hat\theta^{(B)}$ be the bootstrap estimates. Then

$$
\widehat{SE}_{boot}(\hat\theta) \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\left(\hat\theta^{(b)}-\bar{\theta}\right)^2}
}
$$

where

$$
\bar{\theta}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\hat\theta^{(b)}.
$$

Practical notes emphasized in the course materials
1. Choice of $B$: there isn’t a single magic number; “a few thousand” is typically fine.
2. Randomness: bootstrap results vary run-to-run unless you set a random seed.
3. When it can go wrong: small samples, very skewed “extreme value” outcomes, and dependence across observations (panel data, autocorrelation) can break the standard “resample rows iid” approach and may require variants.

The money multiplier is the link between an increase in the monetary base (new reserves injected by the Fed) and the total increase in the money supply $M$ once banks re-lend deposits.

Start from the money definition in the notes:

$$
M = CU + \sum DD
$$

where $CU$ is currency held by the public and $DD$ is demand deposits.

Simple case in the notes: nobody holds cash, so $CU=0$, and banks hold a constant reserve ratio $RR$ (reserves as a fraction of deposits). Then each new dollar of reserves supports a larger amount of deposits because banks keep only fraction $RR$ and lend the rest repeatedly:

$$
m = \frac{1}{RR}
$$

and the basic relationship is:

$$
\Delta M = m \cdot \Delta \text{Reserves}
$$

Intuition: a higher $RR$ means banks “leak” more into reserves each round, so the lending chain dies out sooner, making $m$ smaller. Also, if people hold more cash (higher $CU$ relative to deposits), that’s another “leak” that reduces the multiplier because fewer dollars stay in the banking system to become deposits.

A two-sided market is a setting where ONE platform serves TWO distinct user groups, and demand on each side depends on participation on the other side (cross-side network effects). A clean way to write that is

$$Q_A = D_A(p_A, Q_B), \qquad Q_B = D_B(p_B, Q_A)$$

where $p_A$ and $p_B$ are the prices the platform charges each side, and $Q_A, Q_B$ are participation levels (users, transactions, subscribers, etc.). The platform’s objective is typically

$$\pi = (p_A - c_A)Q_A + (p_B - c_B)Q_B - F$$

so it chooses a PRICE STRUCTURE $(p_A, p_B)$, not just a single price, because cutting price on one side can raise $Q$ on the other side and increase total profit. This is why you often see one side subsidized (low or zero price) while the other side pays more: the subsidized side is valuable because it “brings” the other side. 

In the course’s vertical-channel framing (supplier–my firm–customer), two-sidedness is basically the case where “my firm” is acting like a platform that cares about having many participants on BOTH sides, not just bargaining with a single supplier or a single customer.
